occurrenceRemarks: The broad-winged hawk, also known as the Buteo platypterus, is found in the forests of eastern North America, including North Carolina. This species is a medium-sized prey bird with broad, rounded wings, and a short tail with black and white bands, and brown upperparts with lighter underparts. They hunt from perches in wooded areas and feed on small mammals, reptiles, amphibians, smaller birds, and large insects. During the fall, they migrate in large flocks known as kettles that contain thousands of birds flying together to rising warm currents. They breed in forested habitats in North Carolina during the warmer months before moving south for the winter.

occurrenceRemarks: This Red-shouldered Hawk splashed and preened in the pond like it was a birdbath. He or she stood on one wall for a few minutes, then got in and splashed around, got out on the other side, got back in and splashed, then went back to the first side. The featured photo shows the feathers suddenly held close, creating a slimmer appearance than just a moment before. The fifth and sixth photos show the nictitating membrane (third eyelid). After this extravagant bath, the Hawk perched in a nearby dogwood and then a pine tree, scanning the pond area and surrounding woods for at least 45 minutes. I've never seen such a large bird in the pond.

occurrenceRemarks: Date: 2/7/2023 I traveled 1 mile. Start time 12:55, end time 1:50. It was sunny outside and felt nice with a cool breeze once in a while. I was alone when I saw this species. occurrenceRemarks: To me this was a funny sequence of events. This is the same bird that I had slipped around in the field earlier. When I first came to this particular location searching for tracks I noticed a Northern Mockingbird slightly perturbed with my presence, but not acting overly concerned. In fact, I watched it fly across the old logging road in front of me during my track search. On my way out of the location I suddenly heard the bird start giving vocal alarm calls. Without thinking, I instantly froze. I then saw looking through the Rosebay Rhododendrons to my left an approaching Wild Turkey and the familiar black/ brown coloration around the wings. The bird hesitated and then came on. When it hesitated, I thought it had heeded the Mockingbird’s warnings. (I am sure the Mockingbird was trying to warn the Turkey about my presence instead of the other way around). The Turkey must have just thought the bird was disturbed at its presence and thus it kept coming, not realizing I was there. So, I just held my cellphone camera at the spot I knew it would appear. If I still hunted Wild Turkeys as I used to, and this had been 10 days earlier during the Turkey season…even I wouldn’t have missed this bird at this range and would have harvested a nice Tom without making a single call. Although I would probably have had to do some parboiling on this tough old bird to make it tender to the palate:) The first photo is the birds first appearance. The second photo is when the bird recognizes my silhouette for what it is. The third and final photo is the bird leaving the area for fairer climates. The bird was not overly scared though because it never flew, and I have seen them move away much faster if really frightened.

occurrenceRemarks: The northern cardinal, also known as the Cardinalis cardinalis, is a common songbird seen throughout North Carolina and eastern and central North America. The males are a bright red with a black mask around their face, and females are light brown with red highlights on their crest, tail, and wings. These cardinals live in forests, woodlands, gardens, neighborhoods, and parks where they feed on seeds, insects, and fruit. They are known as the North Carolina state bird, and their chirps can be identified by their clear, whistling songs, which they use to communicate and defend their territory. These birds are nonmigratory and can be seen in North Carolina year-round.

occurrenceRemarks: Spotted this nest with eggs when I was watering the Virginia Cedar that it is in. I was clearly leaves and pinestraw from the upper part of the tree and almost but not quite grabbed the nest. I took the photo above and backed off. The second photo shows the context, with the nest to the right side of the trunk. I planted three cedars along this fence 18 months ago and feel fulfilled as a wildlife gardener now! This is my 1000th iNat observation. Thanks for being part of the community.
identificationRemarks: Congrats on the observations! This brought a smile to my face. Your nest belongs to a Northern Cardinal. They build somewhat flimsy open cup nests of a variety of materials, often placing them in bushes or evergreens. Their eggs are cool in color, blue-ish off-white with brown spots concentrated at one end. Their eggs do look similar to Brown-headed Cowbird eggs - which are obligate brood parasites - so it's hard to tell whether these are cardinal or cowbird.

occurrenceRemarks: https://photos.app.goo.gl/UEddswHnYoFjFnP29 The above link is a video that I shot in order to obtain a sound file to use in the Audacity program. The second two photo's of this female Pileated Woodpecker shows her nest location. The story behind this observation is typical of nesting birds with young at this time of year: As I was walking up this old woods road, a Pileated Woodpecker flew right over my head as I watched it approach from well ahead of me first. Then it landed on this Eastern White Pine that I had walked by a few steps earlier. As it was on the side of the tree you could see that the crest doesn't extend as far to the front as the male. Then after walking up the hill several more steps, I noticed her nest hole about 100 feet past where she had flown over my head and about at the same height off the ground as her fly over and landing on the white pine in the photo. It just makes you realize that the wildlife knows you are in the woods before you realize yourselve that you are in the woods :) They live here 24/7...we are just infrequent visitors. Although she was being very vocal while on the side of the tree, I was only able to get this one recording for sound in the video. They can detect electronics...and that means most wildlife in the woods...don't ask me how specifically though.

occurrenceRemarks: I was walking my dog and this hummingbird suddenly flew to the ground in front of me. I got very close to it and it didnt move. I thought it might be exhausted from the heat (which has happened at my house before) so i picked it up to move it to a shady area but it flew out of my hand before i could even take a picture. I was worried about bird flu so i immediately washed my hands very well. (Im aware of the MBTA and absolutely didnt intend to hurt or keep the bird, but i did pick it up in order to help it. Im not 100% sure if i was allowed to do that but i did what i thought was right in the moment, and of course washed my hands well after)

occurrenceRemarks: Scientific Name – Selasphorus platycercus Common Name – Ruby-throated Hummingbird Location – Kaylane, Lane, Thomasville, NC Date – August 20 Number of Individuals – 1 bird Brief description: It is a medium sized hummingbird that can be seen all over the eastern North America and parts of South America. The males in this species have red-purple gorgets, which means the one in this photograph is most likely a female. They are about 7-9 centimeters long and weigh about 3 and a half grams. Their main diet consist of insects and the nector of flowers. They build nest and live in trees or other elevated safe places. The female lays two eggs that hatch in a couple of weeks.
